description_full: Star Group, L.P., together with its subsidiaries, provides home heating oil and propane products and services to residential and commercial customers in the United States. It offers gasoline and diesel fuel; and installs, maintains, and repairs heating and air conditioning equipment and ancillary services. As of September 30, 2025, the company served approximately 406,400 full-service residential and commercial home heating oil and propane customers and 63,200 customers on a delivery only basis. It sells gasoline and diesel fuel to approximately 27,700 customers. The company was formerly known as Star Gas Partners, L.P. and changed its name to Star Group, L.P. in October 2017. The company was incorporated in 1995 and is based in Stamford, Connecticut.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3K people. Revenue per employee of $590K ranks in the bottom quartile among Energy peers. Each employee generates $19K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Star Group L.P. is a small-cap energy business with a $429M market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -4% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Gross margins of 28% are the starting point for assessing pricing power.

The business throws off $56M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.97× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.9×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 15% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Operating margins 9% below sector median — a cost disadvantage the moat cannot hide
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 6% operating margin trails the Energy median (16%) by 9pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.59x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-33.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 16% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 16% and a beta of 0.42, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $219K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 32% in the 2020 crash, 27% in the 2022 bear market and 54% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 67% below its DCF fair value of $39.68, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 56%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $32.20 to $49.83 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 5.8 vs 13.6, EV/EBITDA 4.0 vs 7.1 and P/FCF 7.7 vs 14.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 7% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 13.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 17.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 13.8% annual cash-flow growth, 19pp less than the model expects.
prof: It runs a 28% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.1x net debt to EBITDA ($24.7M of cash against $188.1M of debt), with interest covered 5.9x.
The current ratio of 0.59 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.8% over 3 years, 4.0% over 5 years and 0.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
Free cash flow has compounded -19.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (0.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has missed earnings estimates by 21.9% on average.
own: Insiders own 15.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 42%.
It returns 6.1% a year to shareholders (6.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 17 consecutive years, raising it 1.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 3,024 employees, each generates about $590K of revenue, 0.3x the Energy median.
That works out to $19K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.4M (2x revenue per employee).

why: DCF is 257% above the other models' median ($13.29)
